q-sop-01.A code-compliance inspection of the home: Ask whether a home inspector is acting as a building official here, and what the SOP says the inspection is not.
q-sop-01.A technically exhaustive evaluation with: Consider how far a standard inspection is expected to go, and whether it promises measurements and calculations on every system.
q-sop-01.An appraisal of the home's overall condi: Think about who puts a dollar value on a house, and whether value ever belongs in an inspection report.

q-sop-02.Walk on the roof surface: Separate what the SOP lets you do from what it requires. Is getting onto the roof surface ever mandatory?
q-sop-02.Predict the remaining service life of th: Can anyone standing on a roof today promise how many years it has left? Check whether forecasting is part of the job.
q-sop-02.Perform a water test on suspected leaks: Think about whether the SOP asks you to recreate a leak, or only to report what you can already observe.

q-sop-03.Nothing; NC adopts the InterNACHI SOP sm: The question says NC adds something. Recall whether the NC rule goes further than InterNACHI on smoke alarms.
q-sop-03.Verify each alarm is hardwired and inter: Think about what an inspector can verify without opening walls or bringing test aerosols, and what the NC rule actually asks.
q-sop-03.Report the battery type and replace each: Would an inspector be servicing equipment on the job? Recall whether NC asks you to repair anything at all.

q-sop-04.Acceptable, because the test button soun: Ask what a sounding test button really proves, and which parts of the alarm it never checks.
q-sop-04.Not reportable, since alarm age is outsi: Look at the label date again. Does the inspection standard stop you from reporting a condition you can plainly read?
q-sop-04.Recommend replacing the battery and rete: The horn already sounded on test. Ask what problem a new battery would actually solve here.

q-sop-05.In the hallway outside the bedrooms and: That pattern matches an older rule. Recall which rooms the current model code added that this list leaves out.
q-sop-05.On each story at the top of the stairs,: Think about what happens to an alarm placed near cooking, and whether the code wants alarms there.
q-sop-05.In each bedroom and in the kitchen, but: Picture the path from a bedroom to the exit, and ask whether the kitchen is a spot the code wants an alarm.

q-sop-06.A basement, a crawlspace, or an open-air: Ask what actually produces carbon monoxide. Does a crawlspace or an open carport make any?
q-sop-06.Bedrooms on more than one story, or a fi: That sounds like a smoke alarm placement rule. Ask what feature of a home makes carbon monoxide possible at all.
q-sop-06.An electric furnace, a heat pump, or a d: Ask whether an electric heater or a heat pump burns anything, and whether a separate building shares the home's air.

q-sop-07.An exterior-grade door of whatever mater: Weatherstripping stops drafts. Ask what this door is really there to slow down, and whether any material will do.
q-sop-07.Solid wood at least 2 in thick, or a 45-: Check both numbers against the course. These figures sound protective, but are they the ones the course actually names?
q-sop-07.Hollow-core wood with a self-closer and: Picture a garage fire reaching a hollow-core door. How long would it hold, closer or not?

q-sop-08.Acceptable, provided the flap is rigid p: Ask what the door is separating, and whether a plastic flap could hold back fire the way the door does.
q-sop-08.A concern when a bedroom opens directly: Ask whether the door's job depends on which room is on the other side, or applies to every garage-to-house door.
q-sop-08.Cosmetic damage to the door, which the S: Is this damage only about looks? Think about what the solid door is there to do.

q-sop-09.1/4 in gypsum board: This is a memorized minimum. Recall the figure the course gives for the walls, separate from the one for a room above.
q-sop-09.3/8 in gypsum board: Thin boards are common in older homes. Check your memory of the course figure, not what you have seen installed.
q-sop-09.1 in gypsum board: That exceeds what the course asks. Recall the minimum for the walls, and the different one for a ceiling under a bedroom.

q-sop-10.Flexible duct with a foil jacket, sealed: Ask whether a foil jacket would survive a garage fire, and what material the course wants in the garage.
q-sop-10.Ductboard or flex, provided the penetrat: Fire caulk protects the hole. Ask what protects the length of duct sitting inside the garage itself.
q-sop-10.Thin aluminum duct, with a register to h: Think about what a register in the garage lets travel into the house's duct system, besides heat.

q-sop-11.Operators over 10 years old, which shoul: Check whether operator age appears anywhere in the NC list of required reports for this item.
q-sop-11.Nothing, since garage door operators are: Recall whether NC treats the garage door operator as excluded, or names specific conditions you must report.
q-sop-11.The condition of the remote transmitters: Recall whether the NC rule mentions the remote transmitters at all, and if so, in which direction.

q-sop-12.12 in above the floor: This is a memorized maximum. Recall the course figure instead of the height that looks typical on most installs.
q-sop-12.18 in above the floor: Picture a small child lying flat under the closing door. Would a beam at that height cross their body?
q-sop-12.24 in above the floor: Picture a pet lying under the door. Ask whether a beam at knee height would ever see it.

q-sop-13.Can be reached by whatever means the ins: Ask whether owning a tall ladder should expand what counts as accessible, and whether the definition depends on equipment at all.
q-sop-13.Is within 6 ft of the floor and not behi: That mixes in a number from another rule. Check whether the InterNACHI glossary definition uses any distance at all.
q-sop-13.Has been made available by the seller in: Ask whether accessibility depends on paperwork from the seller, or on conditions at the house during the inspection.

q-sop-14.A six-foot stepladder: The NC rule names one specific ladder size. Recall that exact size instead of the one you might own.
q-sop-14.An extension ladder at the eave: Ask whether a panel reached from an eave ladder sounds like something anyone would call readily openable.
q-sop-14.The ladder the inspector carries: If the limit depended on each inspector's own ladder, would two inspectors agree on what is readily openable?

q-sop-15.A system that does not function as inten: Ask whether a client would expect to hear that something is not working. Is that ever optional?
q-sop-15.Which systems were not inspected, and wh: Think about how a client would know what you skipped. Is that disclosure optional or required?
q-sop-15.The water supply piping material: Ask whether describing the materials you saw is part of the job, or something the SOP sets aside.

q-sop-16.Within 24 hours after the inspection: That is a fast turnaround many inspectors offer. Recall what the statute sets when the contract gives no date.
q-sop-16.Within five calendar days after the insp: Recall the exact default the statute sets when the agreement is silent, rather than a figure that sounds reasonable.
q-sop-16.Before the due diligence period ends: Due diligence dates come from the purchase contract. Ask whether the inspection statute ties delivery to that date.

q-sop-17.Cost estimates for each listed repair, g: Recall the general exclusions. Are repair costs something an NC inspector is required to provide?
q-sop-17.The safety hazards alone, ranked from mo: Ask whether the summary is limited to one category of finding, and whether the statute requires ranking anything.
q-sop-17.A pass/fail grade for each system and an: Ask whether the statute asks inspectors to grade houses, or to describe conditions they found.

q-sop-18.Cite the current code edition and sectio: Citing a code edition is a claim. Ask whether a house built years ago can fairly be held to the edition published today.
q-sop-18.Obtain written approval from the local b: Ask whether the statute routes your report through a local official, or puts its requirements on you, the inspector.
q-sop-18.Nothing extra, since code citations are: The question says the statute requires something. Recall why most NC reports avoid quoting code at all.

q-sop-19.120 hours of online academic instruction: Ask whether NC licensing includes any hands-on training beyond classroom study.
q-sop-19.200 hours: 80 classroom and 120 field, i: Check the split. Which half of the training is larger, the academic hours or the field hours?
q-sop-19.40 hours of classroom study plus 50 insp: Recall the total hour requirement in rule .1021, and whether it is counted in inspections or in hours.

q-sop-20.Expires each second year on June 30; 24: Recall whether NC licenses renew yearly or less often, and the month the license expires.
q-sop-20.Expires December 31 each year; 16 CE hou: Check the expiration month and the name of the required course. Is it a code update or something else?
q-sop-20.Expires each third year on your birthday: Ask whether NC ties renewal to one fixed date for everyone, or to each licensee's birthday.

q-sop-21.$100,000 errors and omissions coverage,: Ask whether NC requires general liability coverage, and recall the dollar figure tied to it.
q-sop-21.$1,000,000 general liability, with no bo: Recall the general liability figure NC sets, and whether that coverage stands alone or needs a partner.
q-sop-21.A $5,000 surety bond, with no liability: Recall whether a bond alone satisfies NC, or whether some liability coverage is always required.

q-sop-22.Reporting a safety concern that goes bey: Ask whether the SOP sets a floor or a ceiling. Can telling a client more ever breach ethics?
q-sop-22.Telling a client that you also hold an e: Ask whether being open about your other credentials creates a conflict, or simply informs the client.
q-sop-22.Excluding a system from the inspection a: Ask who controls the scope of the inspection, and whether a written request from the client changes it.

q-sop-23.You may, as long as your price is fair a: Ask whether a fair, written price removes the conflict of being paid to fix what you just reported.
q-sop-23.You may not, unless you hold a general c: Ask whether the ethics rule is about having the skill to do the repair, or about something else.
q-sop-23.You may, if you disclose the arrangement: Disclosure helps in many conflicts. Ask whether it fixes this one, where your findings create your own paid work.

q-sop-24.One unit: Think about duplexes and small multiplexes. Do the standards cover only single-family houses?
q-sop-24.Two or fewer units: Recall the exact unit count where residential standards stop and commercial inspection begins.
q-sop-24.Six or fewer units: Recall the exact unit count where the residential standards end. Small apartment buildings may fall outside it.

q-sop-25.Half of each component type, spread acro: Ask whether NC defines this term with a percentage, or with a count tied to location.
q-sop-25.Each readily accessible component, room: If you had to check every one, would the term representative be needed at all?
q-sop-25.Three per floor inside, and two per side: NC defines this term exactly. Recall both counts from the rule rather than numbers that feel thorough.

q-sop-26.After 7 days: Recall the waiting period in the statute. A one-week gap would let candidates retest almost at once.
q-sop-26.After 30 days: Recall the exact waiting period in G.S. 143-151.57(b) rather than a typical retest window from other exams.
q-sop-26.After one year: Ask whether NC makes a candidate wait a full year, or a shorter set period, between attempts.

q-sop-27.The National Home Inspector Examination: Many states use a national exam, and some websites say NC does too. Check what the Board's current documents describe.
q-sop-27.A 100-question open-book exam on the IRC: Recall the format details: number of questions, open or closed book, time allowed, and the passing percentage.
q-sop-27.A field practical exam graded on site by: Field skills are covered in pre-licensing training. Ask whether the licensing exam itself is written or hands-on.

q-sop-28.Building science, Business practices, Re: Ask whether the exam is organized around business skills, or around the systems and standards you inspect.
q-sop-28.IRC chapters 1 through 11, plus the NC B: Ask whether the exam is organized by code chapters, and whether NC inspectors inspect to code at all.
q-sop-28.Electrical, Plumbing, Mechanical, and St: Recall whether pests fall inside the inspector's required scope, and whether this list leaves out a major block.

q-sop-29.Describe, Diagnose, Implication, Disclos: Check the second and last words. Does an inspector diagnose, and does the last step tell the client what to do?
q-sop-29.Document, Determine, Inspect, Direction: Ask whether inspect makes sense as a step after you have already found the defect.
q-sop-29.Detect, Describe, Implication, Deferral: Check the order: would you describe a component before or after detecting a problem? And is deferral the goal?

q-sop-30.Yes, NC requires the garage-to-house doo: The national IRC says yes. Ask whether NC's version of R302.5.1 copies that sentence, or differs from it.
q-sop-30.Yes, when the door has a glass panel or: A pet door is a fire separation issue. Ask whether it changes whether a closer is required.
q-sop-30.Yes, for homes permitted after 2009, whe: Recall which code edition governs now, and what the State Fire Marshal said that edition requires.

q-sop-31.No contract, since the house is unoccupi: Ask whether a house being unfinished changes the paperwork rules that apply to every NC inspection.
q-sop-31.A copy of the building permit and the bu: Ask whether the rule's requirement is about the builder and the permit, or about you and your client.
q-sop-31.A verbal agreement with the builder cove: Recall whether NC accepts verbal agreements for a regular home inspection, then ask why pre-drywall would differ.

q-sop-32.Interior paint and trim finish: Ask what a pre-drywall visit is racing against. Is paint even on the walls yet?
q-sop-32.Appliance operation: Are appliances installed and running while the walls are still open? Think about what is about to be hidden.
q-sop-32.Landscape irrigation: Ask whether landscape systems get covered up by drywall, which is what this rule is built around.

q-sop-33.Whether you entered the space, and how l: Ask whether time spent inside tells a reader how much of the space you really saw.
q-sop-33.Nothing more, as long as you note that t: The question says something changed on June 1, 2026. Ask whether a note alone would satisfy the amended rule.
q-sop-33.The square footage of each space, plus t: Ask whether the amendment is about measuring and cataloguing the space, or about something else a report reader needs.

q-ea-01.Acceptable, as long as both conductors a: Ask whether matching gauge solves the real issue: can one screw clamp two conductors reliably?
q-ea-01.Monitor it; double taps are common in ol: Ask whether a condition being common in older panels makes it safe, or just familiar.
q-ea-01.Recommend replacing the main breaker wit: Ask whether the main breaker has anything to do with two wires under one branch breaker screw.

q-ea-02.Each ground needs its own terminal; neut: Check which conductor carries normal current. Which one would disturb another circuit if it loosened?
q-ea-02.Two same-size conductors may share a ter: Ask whether the rule treats neutrals and grounds the same way, or differently.
q-ea-02.Neutrals and grounds each need their own: Ask whether the rule is that strict for both conductor types, and what the panel label might permit.

q-ea-03.They lower the panel's amperage rating u: Ask whether an open hole in sheet metal can change how much current the panel can carry.
q-ea-03.They ventilate the panel and should be l: Ask whether panels are designed to breathe through knockouts, and what else could come in through them.
q-ea-03.They are cosmetic, since the dead front: Picture where the dead front sits. Does it cover the side walls of the cabinet too?

q-ea-04.When it is landed on a 15 A breaker serv: Ask whether breaker size or circuit use has anything to do with what a white conductor signals.
q-ea-04.When the panel is a subpanel, where whit: Ask whether a subpanel changes what wire colors mean to the next person who works there.
q-ea-04.When it is a separate white wire run in: Ask whether you have the allowance backwards. Which wiring method does the code let you re-mark, and which not?

q-ea-05.Residential panels do not require a circ: Ask how anyone would find the right breaker in an emergency without a directory.
q-ea-05.The labels should be engraved or printed: Ask whether the problem is how the labels were written, or what they actually say.
q-ea-05.The directory should list wire gauge and: Ask what someone shutting off a circuit in a hurry needs to read. Is wire gauge it?

q-ea-06.The panel's manufacture date and the rec: Recall history matters for some panels. Ask whether it explains the rust and water tracks you are looking at.
q-ea-06.Signs of a lightning strike or surge, an: Ask whether a surge leaves water tracks, and what the seller's history could actually confirm for you.
q-ea-06.Nothing more; rust inside a panel is cos: Rust needs water. Ask whether water inside an electrical panel is ever just a cosmetic note.

q-ea-07.Safety hazard; the aluminum wiring shoul: Ask whether all aluminum wiring carries the same fire history, or only one kind in one place.
q-ea-07.Major defect; refer for a derating calcu: With no damage or overheating, ask what evidence would justify calling this a major defect.
q-ea-07.Report it as single-strand aluminum bran: Look at the stem again. Are these conductors solid or stranded, and are they branch wiring or service?

q-ea-08.Normal, since breakers under load are ex: Ask whether one breaker much hotter than its neighbours is ever just normal warmth.
q-ea-08.An overloaded circuit; recommend a large: Ask whether a thermal image can tell you the cause, and what a larger breaker does to the wire it protects.
q-ea-08.A failed breaker that the seller should: Ask whether the camera proves the breaker failed, or only shows heat that could have several causes.

q-ea-09.8 ft: Recall the clearance ladder from the course. Is any rung of it as low as this one?
q-ea-09.10 ft: That rung exists, but ask which kind of traffic it covers. Do cars use a driveway?
q-ea-09.18 ft: That rung exists too. Ask what kind of road and vehicle it is set for.

q-ea-10.18 in: Ask whether a person leaning out a window or over a deck rail could reach this far.
q-ea-10.6 ft: This is a single memorized figure. Recall the course number for reach from decks and windows, not a guess.
q-ea-10.10 ft: Ten feet appears in the vertical clearance ladder. Ask whether this question is about height overhead or reach sideways.

q-ea-11.It absorbs thermal expansion and contrac: Ask what the loop's low point does to anything running along the conductor toward the house.
q-ea-11.It gives the utility slack to disconnect: Ask whether the loop's shape does a job for the house, or only for the line crew at the pole.
q-ea-11.It bonds the service drop to the house g: Ask whether a loop of insulated conductor could connect anything to the grounding system.

q-ea-12.18 in: Picture yourself standing at the open panel with a flashlight. Could you work in that depth safely?
q-ea-12.24 in: That is how far the boxes sit now. Ask whether the required depth matches the problem in the stem.
q-ea-12.48 in: Recall the exact working depth from the course rather than a generous round number.

q-ea-13.Equipment ground: Grounded and grounding sound alike. Ask which of the two carries normal current back to the source.
q-ea-13.Hot: Ask whether the hot is ever described as grounded. What would that word say about its voltage?
q-ea-13.Grounding electrode conductor: Grounded and grounding are different words. Ask which one the electrode conductor belongs to.

q-ea-14.Combined on one bar, the same way as in: Ask how many times neutral and ground are supposed to be bonded in a system, and where.
q-ea-14.Separated, with the neutral bar bonded t: Ask what a bond at the neutral bar would put on the subpanel's metal enclosure.
q-ea-14.Combined, as long as the subpanel has it: Ask whether a main breaker in the subpanel makes it the service, or leaves it downstream equipment.

q-ea-15.Leave the cover on and judge the panel b: Ask whether NC lets you judge a panel from the outside, or expects you to look in.
q-ea-15.Remove the cover with a licensed electri: Ask whether NC asks you to bring another tradesperson along, or sets a rule for you alone.
q-ea-15.Remove the cover when the client request: Ask whether the panel interior is something the client opts into, or part of the standard itself.

q-er-01.Kitchen countertops and bathrooms, by ro: Ask whether NC draws the zone by room labels, or by something you could measure.
q-er-01.Those installed after 1990, when GFCI ru: Ask whether NC ties this report to the age of the house at all.
q-er-01.Bathrooms, kitchens, and garages, but no: Ask whether outdoor receptacles, which sit in rain and wet soil, would be left out of a shock rule.

q-er-02.Acceptable if the receptacle tests GFCI: Ask what GFCI protection does, and whether it keeps rain out of the box.
q-er-02.Cosmetic damage to the cover, which the: Ask what that cover is for. Is its job about looks, or about keeping something out?
q-er-02.Monitor it, unless the receptacle shows: Ask whether you should wait for corrosion to appear before reporting what lets water in.

q-er-03.The receptacle will not power anything u: Ask whether a reversed receptacle still runs a lamp. If it does, why might no one notice?
q-er-03.It matters for 240 V appliances, not for: Think about a lamp's screw shell. Which conductor is it designed to touch?
q-er-03.It makes the upstream GFCI trip whenever: Ask whether a GFCI reacts to which slot is hot, or to current leaking away somewhere.

q-er-04.Nothing; a 'correct' reading means the r: Ask what a three-light tester actually measures, and whether it could be fooled.
q-er-04.Reversed polarity, which this tester doe: Recall what the three-light tester can detect. Is reversed polarity one of its readings?
q-er-04.An open neutral hidden behind the tester: Ask whether the tester would show correct with an open neutral, or flag it.

q-er-05.Acceptable, because the receptacle still: Ask what the third prong promises, and whether working power proves that promise is kept.
q-er-05.Correct it yourself with a three-to-two: Ask whether an inspector repairs things, and whether an adapter supplies a ground that is not there.
q-er-05.Acceptable if a surge protector is plugg: Ask where a surge protector sends the energy it diverts, and whether that path exists here.

q-er-06.Acceptable, because the receptacle still: Ask whether delivering power is the GFCI's special job, or whether it has another one.
q-er-06.Reset it, retest once, and mark it accep: The test button did nothing. Ask whether resetting a device that never tripped proves anything.
q-er-06.Recommend an AFCI breaker for the kitche: Ask whether an AFCI does the same job as a GFCI, or guards against a different hazard.

q-er-07.They are the same device, sold under two: If they were the same device, why would anyone need two names and two kinds of protection?
q-er-07.A GFCI guards against overloads; an AFCI: Ask which device in the panel already handles overloads and short circuits.
q-er-07.A GFCI is for 240 V circuits; an AFCI is: Ask whether these devices are sorted by voltage, or by the hazard each one watches for.

q-er-08.Do not report it, because a 1987 house i: Ask whether NC's rule on ground-fault reporting depends on when the house was built.
q-er-08.Acceptable, because the receptacle's pol: Ask whether correct polarity has anything to do with shock protection near water.
q-er-08.Note it as informational, since GFCI rul: Ask whether missing shock protection beside a sink is something a client would treat as just information.

q-er-09.Closet lights are excluded unless the cl: Ask whether the SOP sorts closet fixtures by closet size or switch type.
q-er-09.It wastes energy; recommend an LED bulb: Ask whether energy use is the concern here, or whether the bulb's position matters more.
q-er-09.Acceptable if the bulb is under 60 watts: Ask whether a smaller bulb stays cool enough to touch fabric safely for hours.

q-er-10.Acceptable, as long as the tape is intac: Ask what contains sparks and heat if that splice ever fails, tape or something else.
q-er-10.Acceptable in attics, since they are uno: Ask whether being rarely entered makes a hidden splice safer, or simply less noticed.
q-er-10.Monitor it, unless the tape is brittle o: Ask whether you should wait for the tape to fail before reporting an unprotected splice.

q-er-11.Stranded aluminum service entrance condu: Ask which aluminum carries the fire history: big stranded feeders, or a different type in a different place.
q-er-11.Copper nonmetallic sheathed cable from t: Ask whether copper cable from that era is the material NC singles out.
q-er-11.Low-voltage thermostat and doorbell wiri: Ask whether thermostat and doorbell wiring carries enough energy to be a fire concern NC names.

q-er-12.Operate GFCIs within 6 ft of the floor: Recall an earlier NC rule you studied about operating ground-fault devices within a certain height.
q-er-12.Report the presence or absence of smoke: Recall what NC added beyond InterNACHI for smoke alarms. Is reporting them optional?
q-er-12.Describe the service amperage and voltag: Ask whether describing the service size is basic information every electrical section starts with.

q-er-13.Disposals are plug-in appliances, which: Look at the stem again. Is this disposal on a cord and plug, or a cable through a knockout?
q-er-13.It is a concern if the disposal is noisy: Ask whether the cable's protection depends on how the disposal sounds.
q-er-13.It is acceptable when the cable is a fle: Ask whether a cord entering a metal knockout needs protection from the sharp edge too.

q-ca-01.To insulate the floor framing above from: Ask whether a thin plastic sheet lying on the soil could do much insulating.
q-ca-01.To stop termites from tunneling up from: Ask whether termites would be stopped by a thin sheet they can go around at every pier and wall.
q-ca-01.To keep the soil from freezing under the: Ask whether a thin sheet lying on the ground could keep soil from freezing.

q-ca-02.4-mil polyethylene, with seams butted an: Check two details: how the code classifies the material, and whether seams are butted or overlapped.
q-ca-02.15-lb roofing felt, lapped 2 in: Ask whether felt is meant to stop vapor, and how far the code wants seams to overlap.
q-ca-02.Landscape fabric, pinned at the seams: Ask what landscape fabric is designed to let through, and whether that suits a crawlspace floor.

q-ca-03.Normal for a vented crawlspace for a few: Ask whether standing water is ever a normal state for a crawlspace, vented or not.
q-ca-03.Recommend a dehumidifier sized for the c: Ask where the water is coming from. Does a dehumidifier stop it arriving?
q-ca-03.Not reportable, since standing water wil: Ask where evaporating water goes in a closed space under a house, and what it reaches.

q-ca-04.The square footage of the crawlspace, it: Ask whether NC asks inspectors to measure and count in the crawlspace, or to describe something else.
q-ca-04.The type, depth, and R-value of the floo: Insulation is a useful detail. Ask whether .1106 is about the floor above, or about the space itself.
q-ca-04.The date and company name of the last te: Ask whether pest treatment history is something the SOP even requires of you.

q-ca-05.1 sq ft per 50 sq ft, or 1 per 500 with: Check the ratio. Recall the base figure for net vent area, and how much a vapor retarder reduces it.
q-ca-05.1 sq ft per 300 sq ft, with no reduction: Ask whether covering the soil should change how much venting a crawlspace needs.
q-ca-05.1 sq ft per 1,500 sq ft, whether or not: Ask whether bare soil and covered soil release the same moisture, and if the vent rule treats them alike.

q-ca-06.Identify the insect species in the repor: Ask whether naming the insect species is a home inspector's job, or a separate specialist's.
q-ca-06.Perform and report a full wood-destroyin: Ask whether the NC SOP requires a pest inspection, and who is licensed to perform one.
q-ca-06.Leave it out of the report entirely, bec: Ask what a client would want to know about mud tubes you saw, whatever the SOP requires.

q-ca-07.Ducts in crawlspaces are excluded from t: Ask whether ductwork you can see in a crawlspace falls outside the HVAC part of the inspection.
q-ca-07.It is cosmetic, as long as the insulatio: Ask whether an intact jacket matters when the duct itself has come apart at a joint.
q-ca-07.Flex duct is designed to rest on the soi: Ask what soil moisture does to a duct lying on it, and how ducts are meant to be supported.

q-ca-08.6 in: Think about how damp wood gets that close to soil. Recall the code figure for joists.
q-ca-08.12 in: That figure belongs to a different member in the same rule. Which framing piece is it for?
q-ca-08.24 in: Recall the exact code figure for joists rather than a generous safety margin.

q-ca-09.When the crawlspace is dirty, damp, or o: Most crawlspaces are dirty and damp. If that excused entry, how many would ever be inspected?
q-ca-09.When the client is not present to witnes: Ask whether the client's presence has anything to do with your duty to inspect a space.
q-ca-09.When the home is less than 10 years old: Ask whether a builder's warranty changes what the SOP asks you to inspect.
